docs.title: dpdpkit
docs.text:
Open-source building blocks for India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 and DPDP Rules, 2025. dpdpkit provides a consent ledger, versioned notices, rights requests, retention with pre-erasure warnings, and audit evidence. It runs inside your own app, against your own database.

You use Install FastAPI pip install "dpdpkit[fastapi]" Django (v0.4) pip install "dpdpkit[django]" Node, PHP, Java, Go, .NET (v0.5) docker run ghcr.io/dpdpkit-dev/server React front end npm i @dpdpkit/react @dpdpkit/client

Most Data Fiduciary obligations become enforceable on 13 May 2027.

Want dpdpkit run for you, or help setting it up? Join the Cloud waitlist.

docs.title: Principles
docs.text:
• Primitives, not promises. dpdpkit gives you tools. It never claims to make you compliant.
  • Rules as data. Every legal number lives in a versioned policy pack.
  • Fail safe. If a warning is not delivered or a job fails, dpdpkit holds and alerts. It never deletes or files anything on its own.
  • Your data stays with you. Open-source installs never call home.

docs.title: Cloud waitlist
docs.text:
dpdpkit Cloud is the hosted version of dpdpkit: the same consent ledger, notices, rights requests and retention jobs, run for you, plus a hosted privacy portal on your own subdomain. An invite-only beta is planned for mid-2027.

The open-source packages stay free and keep working without Cloud. Join the waitlist if you want:

  • an invite to the Cloud beta,
  • help implementing dpdpkit in your app (a readiness sprint), or
  • to become a design partner: free setup help in exchange for feedback while the toolkit is young.

docs.title: Before you sign up
docs.text:
This form collects personal data, so here is the notice we would expect any dpdpkit user to show.

What we collect Your email address (required). Your organisation, stack and interests if you choose to add them. Why To email you about the Cloud beta, implementation help and the design-partner programme. Nothing else. What we don't do Sell your data, share it with anyone other than the form service named below, add you to other lists, or track you across sites. How long we keep it Until you withdraw, or 12 months after dpdpkit Cloud becomes generally available, whichever comes first. Withdraw Use the unsubscribe link in any email, or write to the address below. Withdrawing is as easy as signing up, and we delete your entry within 7 days. Your rights You can ask for a summary of what we hold, correct it, or have it erased.

Signing up is optional and nothing in the form is pre-ticked. The form records which version of this notice you saw.

docs.title: Consent ledger
docs.text:
Consent events are appended to a SHA-256 hash chain per tenant. Every other state change (requests, schedules, holds) goes to a second, audit chain.

Each row's hash covers its canonical JSON (every field except hash), including seq and the previous row's hash (prev_hash). The first row's prev_hash is 64 zeros. So:

Tampering Detected by A row is edited Its own hash no longer matches (ledger verify) An edited row is re-hashed The next row's prev_hash no longer matches (ledger verify) A row is deleted A gap in seq (ledger verify) The newest rows are cut off, or the chain is rebuilt Comparison with an exported root hash (ledger check-root)
  • dpdpkit ledger verify recomputes both chains. It names the first row whose contents or chain link do not match (exit code 2).
  • dpdpkit ledger root prints the current heads; --out FILE appends them to an anchor file.
  • dpdpkit ledger check-root --anchors FILE confirms the chains still match the newest exported root.

Export the root hash periodically to storage you cannot rewrite. See Anchoring the root hash.

docs.title: Policy packs
docs.text:
Every legal number dpdpkit uses (the 48-hour pre-erasure warning, the one-year log floor, the 90-day grievance ceiling) lives in a versioned YAML pack in dpdpkit-policies. No such number is in code.

dpdpkit policy show
dpdpkit policy diff dpdp-rules-2025.v1 my-pack.yaml

A missing or invalid pack stops dpdpkit from starting. There are no built-in defaults. See Rule to code for every key and its legal source.

docs.title: Retention and erasure
docs.text:
1. Activity (login, contact) restarts each purpose's inactivity clock.
  2. retention.erasure_pre_notice_hours before erasure (48 in the base pack), dpdpkit sends a warning through your notifier.
  3. Erasure runs only after the warning is recorded as delivered, and only once the full warning period has passed since delivery.
  4. Any activity after the warning cancels the erasure.
  5. Failed delivery, missing contact details, a failing erasure handler or a legal hold all move the schedule to needs_attention. A person decides what happens next.
  6. Ledger and audit rows are never erased. They are kept for at least retention.min_log_retention_days.

docs.title: FastAPI quickstart
docs.text:
By the end of this page your FastAPI app will show a consent notice, record per-purpose consent in a tamper-evident ledger, block a feature until the user consents, take rights requests and run erasure schedules. Allow about 30 minutes.

You need Python 3.10+ and an existing FastAPI app. Any SQLAlchemy database works: SQLite for trying it out, Postgres or MySQL in production.

docs.title: 1. Install
docs.text:
pip install --pre "dpdpkit[fastapi]" "dpdpkit-fastapi[scheduler]"

--pre is needed while dpdpkit is in alpha. Add dpdpkit-fastapi[postgres] or [mysql] for a database driver.

docs.title: 2. Describe your purposes
docs.text:
dpdpkit init

This writes dpdpkit.yaml. Open it and change three things:

  • contact: your organisation's name, privacy email and rights page. They appear in every notice and every response to a rights request.
  • purposes: one entry per reason you process personal data. Each lists the data_items it uses and, optionally, a retention rule. The starter file has account (required to run the service, erased after 3 years of inactivity) and marketing (optional, erased when consent is withdrawn).
  • notice: the title, body and links shown with the consent form. Add translations for each language you serve.

These are legal decisions

Which purposes need consent, what the notice says and how long data is kept are decisions for you and your counsel. dpdpkit records and enforces what you configure.

The policy: line pins the rules pack (deadlines, warning periods, log retention). See Policy packs.

docs.title: 3. Wire it into your app
docs.text:
main.py
import os

from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI, Request

from dpdpkit import ConsoleNotifier, Contact
from dpdpkit.fastapi import DPDPKit, require_consent

app = FastAPI()


def current_user(request: Request) -> str | None:
    # Return a stable, non-personal id for the signed-in user (a primary key, not an email).
    return request.headers.get("X-User")  # stand-in: replace with your auth


def staff_role(request: Request) -> str | None:
    # "viewer", "handler" or "admin" for staff; None for everyone else.
    return "admin" if request.headers.get("X-User") == "staff" else None


def contact_for(user_id: str) -> Contact | None:
    # Where to send pre-erasure warnings. Look the user up in your own tables.
    return Contact(email=f"{user_id}@example.in")


dpdp = DPDPKit(
    db_url=os.environ.get("DATABASE_URL", "sqlite:///./app.db"),
    config="dpdpkit.yaml",
    principal_resolver=current_user,
    admin_guard=staff_role,
    contact_resolver=contact_for,
    notifier=ConsoleNotifier(),  # prints messages; use SmtpNotifier in production
    signing_key=os.environ.get("DPDPKIT_SIGNING_KEY", "dev-only"),
    migrate_on_startup=True,
)
dpdp.install(app, prefix="/dpdp")

install() adds the REST endpoints under /dpdp, error handlers, a middleware that records user activity (which resets inactivity clocks), and the admin dashboard mount.

principal_resolver and admin_guard may be sync or async and receive the FastAPI Request, so they can read whatever your auth layer puts on it (request.state.user, a session or a JWT).

migrate_on_startup=True creates and upgrades dpdpkit's tables (all prefixed dpdp_). In production you may prefer to run migrations as a deploy step instead:

dpdpkit migrate --kit main:dpdp       # or: --db-url "$DATABASE_URL"
dpdpkit migrate --sql --db-url postgresql://   # print the SQL for review

Start the app:

uvicorn main:app --reload

docs.title: 4. Show the notice and record consent
docs.text:
Your frontend fetches the current notice and posts the user's choices. Nothing is pre-ticked; each optional purpose is a separate decision.

curl "localhost:8000/dpdp/notices/current?locale=hi"

curl -X POST localhost:8000/dpdp/consents -H "X-User: u_42" -H "content-type: application/json" \
     -d '{"decisions": [{"purpose": "account", "granted": true}, {"purpose": "marketing", "granted": true}]}'

curl localhost:8000/dpdp/consents/me -H "X-User: u_42"
curl localhost:8000/dpdp/consents/me/receipt -H "X-User: u_42"     # signed receipt

Every decision is written to the hash-chained ledger with the notice version and content hash the user saw.

For React, @dpdpkit/react provides <ConsentNotice>, <PreferenceCenter> and <RightsRequestForm> that call these endpoints. Other frontends can use @dpdpkit/client.

docs.title: 5. Gate features on consent
docs.text:
main.py
@app.post("/offers/send", dependencies=[Depends(require_consent("marketing"))])
def send_offer() -> dict[str, bool]:
    return {"sent": True}

Without consent the endpoint returns 403 with {"error": {"code": "consent_required", ...}} naming the purpose, so the frontend can ask for it. In background jobs, check directly:

if dpdp.kit.consent.check(user_id, "marketing"):
    ...

Withdrawal is one call, and it takes effect immediately:

curl -X POST localhost:8000/dpdp/consents/marketing/withdraw -H "X-User: u_42"
curl -X POST localhost:8000/offers/send -H "X-User: u_42"     # 403 consent_required

docs.title: Async apps
docs.text:
If your app uses async SQLAlchemy, give dpdpkit the same URL or engine:

from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import create_async_engine

engine = create_async_engine("postgresql+asyncpg://app:secret@db/app")
dpdp = DPDPKit(engine=engine, ...)          # or db_url="postgresql+asyncpg://..."

dpdpkit's core is synchronous, so it connects with the matching sync driver (asyncpg → psycopg, aiosqlite → sqlite, aiomysql/asyncmy → PyMySQL) through its own small connection pool. Install it with dpdpkit-fastapi[postgres] or [mysql]. The REST endpoints already run in a threadpool. In your own async def code, call kit methods through dpdp.run() so the event loop is never blocked:

@app.post("/newsletter")
async def newsletter(user=Depends(current_user)):
    if await dpdp.run(dpdp.kit.consent.check, user.id, "marketing"):
        ...

docs.title: 6. Tell dpdpkit how to erase and export your data
docs.text:
dpdpkit never touches your own tables. You register two kinds of function:

main.py
@dpdp.kit.retention.register_handler
def erase_user_data(user_id: str, purposes: list[str]) -> None:
    # Delete or anonymise this user's rows for these purposes. Raise if anything fails.
    if "account" in purposes:
        ...  # e.g. db.execute(delete(User).where(User.id == user_id))
    if "marketing" in purposes:
        ...  # e.g. remove them from your mailing list


dpdp.kit.export.register_collector("orders", lambda user_id: {"orders": []})  # your data for access requests

If a handler raises, the erasure is marked needs_attention and nothing is retried until a person resolves it. See Retention and erasure for every fail-safe.

docs.title: 7. Rights requests
docs.text:
Users open requests; staff work them through the admin API (or the admin dashboard from v0.4).

curl -X POST localhost:8000/dpdp/requests -H "X-User: u_42" -H "content-type: application/json" \
     -d '{"kind": "erasure", "details": {}}'

curl "localhost:8000/dpdp/admin/requests?open=true" -H "X-User: staff"

curl -X PATCH localhost:8000/dpdp/admin/requests/<id> -H "X-User: staff" -H "content-type: application/json" \
     -d '{"action": "respond", "message": "Your account data has been erased."}'

Deadlines come from the policy pack. Responding to an erasure request calls your erasure handlers, respecting legal holds and purposes kept under a legal obligation.

docs.title: 8. Run the scheduler
docs.text:
Retention warnings and erasures run on a schedule. In one process (not every web worker):

dpdp.start_scheduler(retention_minutes=15)

This runs retention every 15 minutes, verifies the ledger daily, exports the ledger root hash daily and sends any queued webhooks. Without APScheduler, call the CLI from cron instead:

dpdpkit retention run --kit main:dpdp
dpdpkit ledger verify --kit main:dpdp

docs.title: 9. Check it works
docs.text:
dpdpkit ledger verify --kit main:dpdp              # ok: N rows verified
dpdpkit retention preview --kit main:dpdp          # what will be warned or erased this week
curl localhost:8000/dpdp/me/export -H "X-User: u_42"   # what an access request returns

The full contract is tested by the conformance suite. Point it at your app to check nothing is missing:

pip install --pre "dpdpkit-conformance[asgi]"
DPDPKIT_ASGI_APP=main:app dpdpkit-conformance

The suite authenticates with test headers, so your resolvers must honour them while it runs. See examples/fastapi_shop for the pattern.

docs.title: Before production
docs.text:
• [ ] Replace the stand-in current_user and staff_role with your real auth.
  • [ ] Set DPDPKIT_SIGNING_KEY to a long random secret, kept out of source control.
  • [ ] Use SmtpNotifier, SesNotifier or your own notifier so pre-erasure warnings are actually delivered. See Email delivery.
  • [ ] Register erasure handlers for every purpose that has a retention rule, and test them.
  • [ ] Run the scheduler in exactly one process.
  • [ ] Export the ledger root hash somewhere you cannot rewrite. See Anchoring.
  • [ ] If other systems must act on erasures or withdrawals, configure webhooks.
  • [ ] Have counsel review dpdpkit.yaml: purposes, notice text, translations and retention periods.

docs.title: Any other stack
docs.text: dpdpkit-server runs the FastAPI adapter as a standalone container with its own database. Your backend calls its REST API, and your front end uses @dpdpkit/embed web components. The server ships in v0.5 (tasks SRV-01 to SRV-08).

docs.title: Anchoring the ledger root hash
docs.text:
The hash chain proves that no row was edited or removed from the middle. On its own it cannot prove that the newest rows were not cut off the end, or that someone with database access did not rebuild the whole chain from scratch. A root hash closes that gap: it records the head of each chain at a point in time. Keep a copy somewhere the database operator cannot rewrite, and any later truncation or rebuild no longer matches it.

{
  "tenant_id": "default",
  "consent_head": "9f2c…", "consent_seq": 1841,
  "audit_head": "41ab…",   "audit_seq": 7302,
  "root": "c07e…",
  "exported_at": "2027-06-01T03:00:00Z"
}

A root hash contains only hashes and counters, never personal data, so it is safe to publish.

docs.title: Exporting
docs.text:
CLI (cron, CI, any stack)FastAPI schedulerPython 
# append today's root to a JSON-lines file
dpdpkit ledger root --kit myapp:dpdp --out /mnt/anchors/roots.jsonl

from dpdpkit import FileRootSink

dpdp.start_scheduler(
    root_export_hour=3,                                   # daily, 03:00 UTC (None disables)
    root_sinks=[FileRootSink("/mnt/anchors/roots.jsonl")],
)

root = kit.ledger.export_root(FileRootSink("roots.jsonl"))

Every export also publishes a ledger.root_exported event. Subscribe a webhook to it to hand each root to a third party as it is produced (see Where to keep it).

A sink is any object with a write(root) method, so you can write directly to your own store:

import datetime as dt

import boto3

s3 = boto3.client("s3")


class ObjectLockSink:
    def write(self, root):
        s3.put_object(
            Bucket="acme-dpdp-anchors",
            Key=f"{root.tenant_id}/{root.exported_at:%Y/%m/%d}.json",
            Body=root.model_dump_json(),
            ObjectLockMode="COMPLIANCE",
            ObjectLockRetainUntilDate=root.exported_at + dt.timedelta(days=3 * 365),
        )

If a sink raises, export_root() raises too, so a failed anchor is never skipped silently. The FastAPI job logs the failure and tries again the next day.

docs.title: Checking
docs.text:
dpdpkit ledger verify     --kit myapp:dpdp                                # chain is internally consistent
dpdpkit ledger check-root --kit myapp:dpdp --anchors /mnt/anchors/roots.jsonl

check-root takes the newest root for the tenant and confirms the chains still contain a row at each recorded sequence number with the recorded hash. Because each row includes the hash of the row before it, matching the newest anchor also proves nothing before it changed. Exit codes: 0 ok, 1 no usable anchor, 2 mismatch.

Run both checks on the same schedule as the export, for example right before it.

docs.title: Where to keep it
docs.text:
Pick at least one place you cannot quietly edit. More than one is better.

Option What protects it Effort S3 (or compatible) bucket with Object Lock in compliance mode Not even the account root user can delete or overwrite an object before its retention date Low; use a separate AWS account if you can Webhook to a partner: your auditor, legal counsel or parent company The copy is held by someone else Low; subscribe to ledger.root_exported RFC 3161 timestamp (openssl ts -query, then send it to a public timestamping authority) A signed token showing the root existed at that time Medium OpenTimestamps (ots stamp roots.jsonl) Anchored in the Bitcoin blockchain, free Medium; confirmation takes a few hours Public Git repository Forks and mirrors keep old history; a force-push shows up Low, but weaker: the owner can still rewrite it Local file on the app server Protects against accidents only None

Same credentials, no protection

If the credentials that can write your database can also delete the anchor, the anchor proves nothing. Use a different account, a different owner, or write-once storage.

docs.title: How often
docs.text: Daily is a sensible default. Rows written since the last anchor are protected by the chain alone, so the export interval is the window in which a truncation could go unnoticed. High-volume or regulated deployments can export hourly. The job is cheap: it reads two rows.

docs.title: In an incident or an audit
docs.text: Give the auditor three things: the evidence pack (dpdpkit export --evidence), the anchor file, and the output of dpdpkit ledger check-root. They can recompute every row hash independently. See Consent ledger for the hashing rules.

docs.title: Email delivery
docs.text:
dpdpkit sends one kind of message that has legal weight: the pre-erasure warning (Rule 8). An erasure only runs after its warning is recorded as delivered, and only once the full warning period has passed since that moment. So the notifier you choose decides what "delivered" means.

Notifier "Delivered" means Use it for NullNotifier (default) Never: every send fails Keeps erasure switched off until you choose a transport ConsoleNotifier Printed to the console Local development only SmtpNotifier Accepted by your SMTP relay Any provider with SMTP SesNotifier Accepted by Amazon SES SES without event tracking SesNotifier(track_delivery=True) SES reports the recipient's mail server accepted it The strongest evidence available

docs.title: SMTP
docs.text:
from dpdpkit import SmtpNotifier

notifier = SmtpNotifier("smtp.example.in", 587, sender="privacy@example.in",
                        username=os.environ["SMTP_USER"], password=os.environ["SMTP_PASSWORD"])

docs.title: Amazon SES
docs.text:
pip install --pre "dpdpkit[ses]"

from dpdpkit.ses import SesNotifier

notifier = SesNotifier("privacy@example.in", region="ap-south-1")

Credentials come from the usual AWS chain (environment, instance role, ~/.aws). The sender address or its domain must be verified in SES, and the account must be out of the SES sandbox to email anyone.

docs.title: Tracked delivery
docs.text:
With track_delivery=True, a message SES accepts is recorded as queued. The pre-erasure warning does not count, and no erasure clock starts, until SES reports a Delivery event. A Bounce, Reject or Rendering Failure moves the erasure to needs_attention for a person to resolve.

One-time AWS setup:

  1. Create an SES configuration set (for example dpdp) with an event destination that publishes Delivery, Bounce, Reject and Rendering failure events to an SNS topic.
  2. Create an SQS queue and subscribe it to that topic.
  3. Give the app's IAM role ses:SendEmail and, on the queue, sqs:ReceiveMessage and sqs:DeleteMessage.

Then:

from dpdpkit.ses import SesNotifier, poll_ses_events

notifier = SesNotifier("privacy@example.in", region="ap-south-1",
                       configuration_set="dpdp", track_delivery=True)

# every minute, next to the retention job (scheduler, cron or a worker):
poll_ses_events(kit, "https://sqs.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/123456789012/dpdp-ses")

Each message carries a dpdpkit_receipt tag, so events are matched to dpdpkit's delivery receipts. Events for mail dpdpkit did not send are ignored. A queue message is deleted only after its event has been recorded.

Why a queue and not an HTTPS endpoint

A forged "delivered" event would start an erasure clock early. Reading events from SQS with your own AWS credentials means only SES can produce them. If you must receive SNS over HTTPS instead, verify every SNS message signature before calling apply_ses_event.

docs.title: SMS and WhatsApp
docs.text: The built-in notifiers send email only; SMS and WhatsApp messages get a failed receipt. Implement the Notifier protocol (one method, send(message) -> DeliveryReceipt) to use another provider. Return DeliveryStatus.QUEUED when the provider confirms later, and report the outcome with kit.retention.confirm_warning_delivery(receipt_id, delivered).

docs.title: Webhooks
docs.text:
dpdpkit can notify other systems when something happens: a consent is withdrawn, an erasure is due, a rights request is opened. Each notification is an HTTPS POST with a signed JSON body.

With the FastAPI adapter, webhooks go through an outbox in your database:

  1. When an event is published, dpdpkit stores one row per endpoint that wants it. The request that caused the event never waits on the network.
  2. The scheduler sends due rows every 30 seconds.
  3. A failed send (network error or any non-2xx response) is retried with exponential backoff: 30 s, 1 min, 2 min, 4 min… capped at 2 hours, for up to 10 attempts (about 4 hours in total).
  4. After the last attempt the row becomes a dead letter. It stays until someone redelivers it. Nothing is dropped silently.

docs.title: Configure endpoints
docs.text:
dpdpkit.yamlPython 
webhooks:
  - id: crm
    url: https://crm.example.in/dpdp-hooks
    secret_env: CRM_WEBHOOK_SECRET        # the secret itself stays in the environment
    events: [consent.withdrawn, erasure.due]
  - id: audit-log
    url: https://logs.example.in/ingest
    secret_env: AUDIT_WEBHOOK_SECRET      # no `events`: receives everything

from dpdpkit.events import WebhookEndpoint

dpdp = DPDPKit(
    ...,
    webhooks=[
        WebhookEndpoint(id="crm", url="https://crm.example.in/dpdp-hooks",
                        secret=os.environ["CRM_WEBHOOK_SECRET"], events=["consent.withdrawn"]),
    ],
)

Then run the scheduler (dpdp.start_scheduler()), which adds the delivery job whenever an endpoint is configured. Without APScheduler, call dpdpkit webhooks send --kit main:dpdp from cron every minute.

The outbox table is created by dpdpkit migrate (migration 0002).

docs.title: Events
Receiving webhooks
docs.text:
Every request carries three headers:

Header Value X-DPDPKit-Event The event type X-DPDPKit-Delivery The delivery id (stable across retries) X-DPDPKit-Signature t=<unix seconds>,v1=<hex HMAC-SHA256 of "<t>.<raw body>">

Verify the signature over the raw body before parsing it, and reject anything older than five minutes. Respond with any 2xx quickly; do slow work in the background.

PythonNode.js 
from dpdpkit.events import verify_signature

@app.post("/dpdp-hooks")
async def hook(request: Request):
    body = await request.body()
    if not verify_signature(SECRET, body, request.headers.get("X-DPDPKit-Signature", "")):
        raise HTTPException(401)
    event = json.loads(body)
    ...
    return {"ok": True}

import crypto from "node:crypto";

function verify(secret, rawBody, header, toleranceSeconds = 300) {
  const parts = Object.fromEntries(header.split(",").map((p) => p.split("=", 2)));
  const t = Number(parts.t);
  if (!t || !parts.v1 || Math.abs(Date.now() / 1000 - t) > toleranceSeconds) return false;
  const expected = crypto.createHmac("sha256", secret).update(`${t}.`).update(rawBody).digest("hex");
  return parts.v1.length === expected.length &&
    crypto.timingSafeEqual(Buffer.from(parts.v1), Buffer.from(expected));
}

// Express: keep the raw body for verification
app.post("/dpdp-hooks", express.raw({ type: "application/json" }), (req, res) => {
  if (!verify(process.env.DPDP_SECRET, req.body, req.get("X-DPDPKit-Signature") ?? "")) {
    return res.sendStatus(401);
  }
  const event = JSON.parse(req.body);
  res.sendStatus(204);
});

Deliveries can repeat

A delivery is retried whenever dpdpkit does not see a 2xx, including when your endpoint did the work but the response was lost. Use the event id as an idempotency key.

docs.title: Dead letters
docs.text:
dpdpkit webhooks list --kit main:dpdp                 # counts and recent deliveries
dpdpkit webhooks dead --kit main:dpdp                 # what gave up, and the last error
dpdpkit webhooks retry --id wh_… --kit main:dpdp      # one delivery, with a fresh attempt budget
dpdpkit webhooks retry --all --kit main:dpdp

From Python: dpdp.webhooks.dead_letters(), dpdp.webhooks.redeliver(delivery_id) and dpdp.webhooks.counts(). The admin dashboard (v0.4) shows the same list.

A delivery to an endpoint that has been removed from the configuration goes straight to dead letters, so you can see it rather than lose it.

docs.title: Tuning
docs.text:
The defaults suit most installs. To change them, adjust the outbox after creating DPDPKit:

dpdp.webhooks.max_attempts = 15
dpdp.webhooks.max_delay = dt.timedelta(hours=6)

Several processes may run deliver_due() at the same time: each delivery is claimed before it is sent, so it goes out once per attempt.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text:
The code packages (dpdpkit-core, dpdpkit-fastapi, dpdpkit-conformance, @dpdpkit/client, @dpdpkit/react, and later dpdpkit-django and dpdpkit-server) are released together with one version number. Policy packs (dpdpkit-policies) use calendar versions and are released on their own.

Version change Below 1.0 From 1.0 Patch (0.3.1) Fixes only Fixes only Minor (0.4.0) New features; may remove APIs deprecated at least two minors earlier New features, backwards compatible Major (2.0.0) n/a May remove APIs deprecated in an earlier 1.x

Alpha, beta and release-candidate builds (0.3.0a1, 0.3.0-alpha.1) carry no compatibility promise.

docs.title: What is public
docs.text:
• Python: everything importable without a leading underscore from dpdpkit, dpdpkit.<module>, dpdpkit.fastapi and dpdpkit_conformance, as listed in the Python API. Names starting with _ (such as dpdpkit._util) may change in any release.
  • JavaScript: the exports of @dpdpkit/client, @dpdpkit/client/express and @dpdpkit/react.
  • REST: everything in openapi.yaml.
  • CLI: commands, options and exit codes.
  • Database: the dpdp_* tables belong to dpdpkit. Read them if you like, but change them only through dpdpkit migrate.

docs.title: How something is deprecated
docs.text:
1. The release that deprecates it lists it under Deprecated in the changelog, with what to use instead.

  2. Every use emits a DpdpkitDeprecationWarning (a DeprecationWarning) that names the replacement and the release that will remove it:

    DpdpkitDeprecationWarning: Ledger.export_roots() is deprecated since dpdpkit 0.3 and will be
removed in 0.5; use Ledger.export_root() instead

    Deprecated functions and classes are also marked for type checkers (PEP 702), so mypy (with --enable-error-code deprecated) and pyright report callers before the code runs. 3. It keeps working, unchanged, for at least two minor releases and at least 90 days. 4. It is removed in the release named in the warning, and the changelog lists the removal under Removed.

Python hides DeprecationWarning outside test runners and __main__. To see these in your app:

python -W always::DeprecationWarning -m uvicorn main:app
# or in pytest (pyproject.toml): filterwarnings = ["error::dpdpkit.DpdpkitDeprecationWarning"]

docs.title: REST contract
docs.text:
• A deprecated operation or field is marked deprecated: true in openapi.yaml.
  • Responses from a deprecated operation carry a Deprecation header (RFC 9745) and, once a removal date is set, a Sunset header (RFC 8594).
  • Removing or renaming anything in the contract is a breaking change. Pull requests to dpdpkit-spec run a breaking-change check and need the breaking-change label to pass it.

docs.title: Policy packs
docs.text: A published pack id (for example dpdp-rules-2025.v1) is never changed or removed. When the Rules or the Board's guidance change, a new pack id is published and the changelog cites the notification. dpdpkit policy diff shows exactly what moved, and switching packs is a one-line config change.

docs.title: Database
docs.text: Migrations only move forward and never drop consent, audit or ledger data. A column that is no longer used stays until a major version, and the changelog says when it stopped being written.

docs.title: ses
docs.text:
Amazon SES email transport (pip install "dpdpkit-core[ses]").

By default a message SES accepts is reported as delivered, like SmtpNotifier. With track_delivery=True it is reported as queued and tagged with the dpdpkit receipt id; the final outcome comes from SES event publishing (configuration set → SNS → SQS) and is applied with poll_ses_events. A pre-erasure warning then only counts once SES reports the mailbox accepted it.

Events are read from SQS with your AWS credentials rather than received on a public URL: a forged "delivered" event would start an erasure clock, so the channel must be authenticated.

Call a kit method inside the app's AsyncSession, so its writes commit or roll back with the app's own work::

async with AsyncSession(engine) as s, s.begin():
    s.add(Order(...))
    await dpdp.run_in_session(s, dpdp.kit.consent.grant, user_id, "marketing")

docs.title: webhooks
docs.text:
Durable outbound webhooks: a database outbox with retries, backoff and a dead-letter state.

Publishing an event only inserts one row per matching endpoint, so request handlers never wait on the network. WebhookOutbox.deliver_due (run by the scheduler) sends due rows, reschedules failures with exponential backoff, and marks a row dead after max_attempts. Dead rows stay until someone redelivers them; nothing is dropped silently.

Receivers verify X-DPDPKit-Signature with dpdpkit.events.verify_signature and should treat the event id as an idempotency key: a delivery can arrive more than once.

docs.title: WebhookOutbox

max_attempts sends spaced base_delay * 2**n apart (capped at max_delay): with the defaults, 10 attempts over roughly 4 hours. lease stops two workers sending the same row.

docs.title: ledger
docs.text:
Append-only, hash-chained consent ledger and audit trail.

Each tenant has two chains: consent (grant/deny/withdraw events) and audit (every other state change). A row's hash is SHA-256 over its canonical JSON (all fields except hash), which includes prev_hash and seq. Editing a row breaks its own hash; deleting one breaks seq continuity; truncating the tail is caught by comparing with an exported RootHash.

Root hashes are only useful if they are kept somewhere the operator cannot rewrite. Call Ledger.export_root on a schedule with a RootSink, and/or subscribe a webhook to the ledger.root_exported event so a third party holds a copy.

docs.title: deprecation
docs.text:
Deprecation helpers used by every dpdpkit package (see "Deprecation policy" in the docs).

A deprecated API keeps working for at least two minor releases (and at least 90 days) after the release that deprecates it, warns with DpdpkitDeprecationWarning every time it is used, and is listed under "Deprecated" in the changelog.

Functions, methods and classes are marked with PEP 702 so type checkers report callers too. The message must be a string literal (mypy ignores computed messages) in the standard wording::

from typing_extensions import deprecated

@deprecated(
    "Ledger.export_roots() is deprecated since dpdpkit 0.3 and will be removed in 0.5; "
    "use Ledger.export_root() instead",
    category=DpdpkitDeprecationWarning,
)
def export_roots(self): ...

Parameters, config keys and renamed module attributes use warn_deprecated and moved.

docs.title: DpdpkitDeprecationWarning
docs.text:
Bases: DeprecationWarning

Something you use will be removed in a later dpdpkit release. The message says what replaces it.

Python hides DeprecationWarning outside __main__ and test runners; to see these everywhere, run with -W always::dpdpkit.DpdpkitDeprecationWarning.

docs.title: retention
docs.text:
Erasure schedules, pre-erasure warnings, legal holds and processor fan-out (DPDP Rules, Rule 8).

Fail-safe rules enforced here:

  • An erasure runs only after its warning is recorded as delivered, and only once the full warning period (retention.erasure_pre_notice_hours) has passed since delivery.
  • A failed or impossible warning, or a failing erasure handler, moves the schedule to needs_attention. Nothing is retried destructively without a person resolving it.
  • Activity by the principal after the warning cancels an inactivity-based erasure.
  • A legal hold blocks warning and erasure until it is released.
  • Ledger and audit rows are never erased; they are kept at least min_log_retention_days.

docs.title: repository
docs.text:
Storage interface. Each adapter implements Repository with its ORM.

Rules for implementers:

  • Only the models in dpdpkit.models cross this boundary — never ORM rows.
  • Ledger and audit tables are append-only. append_* must raise SequenceConflict when (tenant_id, seq) already exists.
  • Datetimes must round-trip with microsecond precision; naive values are read back as UTC.
  • transaction() groups an audit entry with the state change it describes.
